raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a catheter-based strategy for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF) that mechanically excludes the left atrial appendage (LAA), the dominant site of atrial thrombus in nonvalvular AF. The rationale derives from surgical and echocardiographic observations that most thrombi in nonvalvular AF arise in the LAA, although atrial cardiomyopathy and non-LAA sources of embolism mean LAAC is not a complete substitute for systemic anticoagulation in every patient [1], [2]. Early feasibility experience with the PLAATO system established transseptal endocardial occlusion as technically possible, but contemporary evidence largely concerns nitinol plug-and-disc devices, especially Watchman/Watchman FLX and Amplatzer Amulet [3].

Randomized data initially compared Watchman with warfarin. PROTECT AF demonstrated noninferiority for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular or unexplained death, but with important early procedural complications [4]. In warfarin-ineligible patients, the nonrandomized ASAP study suggested that implantation followed by dual antiplatelet therapy could yield acceptable thromboembolic outcomes, supporting use in patients with bleeding contraindications [5]. Longer PROTECT AF follow-up showed sustained benefit, including lower hemorrhagic stroke and mortality, whereas PREVAIL confirmed improved procedural safety but had inconclusive first coprimary efficacy results because of unexpectedly low ischemic stroke rates in the warfarin group [6], [7]. Patient-level 5-year analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL supported comparable stroke prevention to warfarin with less hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, major nonprocedural bleeding, and mortality [8].

The direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) era has refined patient selection. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC or DOACs, predominantly apixaban, and found LAAC noninferior for a composite of thromboembolic, cardiovascular, bleeding, and device/procedure outcomes; 4-year follow-up preserved noninferiority and suggested less nonprocedural bleeding [9], [10]. In 2026, CHAMPION-AF extended evidence to anticoagulation-eligible patients and found Watchman FLX noninferior to DOACs for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism with less nonprocedural bleeding [11]. Conversely, CLOSURE-AF, enrolling older German patients at high stroke and bleeding risk and comparing LAAC with physician-directed medical therapy, did not meet noninferiority for a broad composite outcome [12]. These apparently divergent trials emphasize that LAAC is not a universal replacement for DOACs; benefit depends on baseline bleeding risk, competing mortality, device generation, endpoint definitions, and postimplant antithrombotic regimens.

Device choice is another evolving issue. In Amulet IDE, Amulet was noninferior to Watchman 2.5 for safety and effectiveness and superior for complete LAA occlusion, but procedural complications were more frequent with Amulet [13]. SWISS-APERO, which incorporated Watchman FLX, showed similar CT-defined residual patency between Amulet and Watchman/FLX, lower transesophageal echocardiographic leak with Amulet, and more early procedural complications [14]. Watchman FLX itself was evaluated in PINNACLE FLX, showing high implant success and low early complication rates, reflecting advances in design, recapturability, and operator experience [15]. Observational Amulet and Watchman registries have reported high implant success in older, higher-risk populations often excluded from pivotal trials [16], [17], [18].

Procedure planning requires careful LAA imaging, usually with transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac CT, to exclude thrombus, define ostial diameter, landing zone, depth, and morphology, and select device size. Implantation is performed by femoral venous access and transseptal puncture, followed by heparinization, angiographic and echocardiographic deployment, tug testing, and assessment for peridevice leak or pericardial effusion. Procedural safety has improved substantially in postapproval practice: early U.S. experience and the NCDR LAAO Registry demonstrated high implantation success with low in-hospital rates of death and stroke, although bleeding, pericardial effusion, device embolization, and vascular complications remain clinically important [19], [20]. One-year NCDR outcomes confirmed that real-world recipients are generally older and at higher bleeding risk than trial participants, making absolute event rates strongly dependent on comorbidity [21].

The main late device-specific concerns are device-related thrombus (DRT), peridevice leak, and residual embolic risk. DRT occurs in a minority of patients but is associated with stroke or systemic embolism, warranting surveillance imaging and intensified antithrombotic therapy when feasible [22], [23], [24]. Postimplant antithrombotic strategies have shifted from warfarin plus aspirin to DOAC-based regimens, dual antiplatelet therapy, or individualized short-course therapy in patients with major bleeding, including prior intracranial hemorrhage [25], [26]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that LAAC may become economically favorable over time in patients who avoid long-term anticoagulant costs and bleeding events, but this depends on procedural cost, life expectancy, and complication rates [27].

Current practice therefore positions percutaneous LAAC for AF patients with elevated stroke risk who have contraindications to, intolerance of, or strong preference against long-term oral anticoagulation after shared decision-making. Technical expertise, standardized imaging, and rigorous follow-up are essential [28]. U.S. and European guidelines endorse LAAC as an option in selected patients, particularly when long-term anticoagulation is unsuitable, while continuing to regard DOACs as first-line therapy for most eligible patients [29], [30].
